title: Lightcraft Review: It’s Adobe Lightroom, Without Adobe
summary: Lightcraft Review: It’s Adobe Lightroom, Without Adobe

sentences: The truth is that Lightcraft really is a free version of Adobe Lightroom — and in some ways it’s better but in other ways it’s just nearly as frustrating.
If you’re aware of the odd headaches that you get sometimes when you’re doing something new, then know that you’re probably going to have that with Lightcraft.
Over a decade ago, I moved away from Lightroom because the Phoblographer has long had issues with Adobe’s ethics and photographers are only now waking up to it.
My typical editing platform is Capture One.
And by all means, I’m sticking with it.
But if I were sick of Adobe and I didn’t want to buy Capture One, then I’d go with Lightcraft with a few bits of understanding.
Last weekend, 2000 people joined us at the 5 Boro Foto Fest in protest of Generative AI coming to replace humans.
If you’ve been sick of Adobe training their algorithms and AI on exactly what you’re doing, then this is a review for you to read.
Extra declarations that you should know besides what I list towards the bottom: Phoblographer hasn’t had advertising with Adobe in over a decade.
So I’m absolutely not afraid of possibly turning down money from them.
Nor do I own any stock in Adobe.
Can your favorite journalists or influencers say the same thing?
Lightcraft is completely free for photographers, so I absolutely think that it’s worth checking out thus far.
It can essentially function like Lightroom.
But it isn’t as robust of a photo editor as Capture One. which I still rate to be better than Lightcraft.
But if you’re sick of Adobe’s crap, give Lightcraft a serious consideration.
This past weekend at the 5 Boro Foto Fest, I spoke with a gentleman about our event’s stance on Generative AI and editing.
He asked about how in Adobe it uses it.
My response to him eventually lead to my asking an important question: if he’s sick of companies training their products on what he does, why didn’t he move away a long time ago?
And that has been a question that I ask every single photographer.
Here are the Phoblographer, our standard is Capture One.
And if you’re a member, then you get a discount to Capture One.
The only thing that’s majorly AI-related that Lightcraft has is AI Denoise; and the fact that the creator of the program used AI to allegedly copy Lightroom with some tweaks to my knowledge.
But otherwise, Lightcraft is the version of Adobe Lightroom we all wanted: something not connected to the cloud and without all the AI editing features.
Granted, that also means that if you’re use to Capture One, you’ll know just how deplorable a photo editor Lightroom is.
And you’ll see it in Lightcraft’s final images.
Somehow the photos still look like AI edited them.
In contrast to Capture One, images still look really natural.
For a free program, Lightcraft is giving Lightroom a run for their money in nearly every single way.
And considering that for over a decade I’ve been critical of Adobe not giving back to photographers more, I think that this is a win for photographers that’s well worth celebrating.
Lightcraft is being awarded four out of five stars.
With a bit more work, I think that it’ll be perfect and worthy of our Editor’s Choice award.
Lightcraft is a free download , and you can check it out on their website.
I’m starting to write this section with a giant sigh.
I downloaded Lightcraft for free, because, well, it’s free.
And then I started editing with it on my 2024 Macbook Pro.
Installation was insanely fast; in fact, it was really odd that it happened all that quickly.
Then it was time to get set up.
Lightcraft doesn’t let me import a Capture One catalog, but I can import a Lightroom catalog.
I haven’t used Lightroom in over a year as I tried it out again and then absolutely hated it and how anti-consumer Adobe’s practices are.
The nomenclature here is really weird.
Libraries are then broken down into their own editing sessions that you call Albums — or at least you should do this.
Expanding the left side section of the editing screen lets you have a whole navigation menu just like Lightroom.
When you’re importing, you need to set it to import images from an entire folder.
This is a rather odd decision — I mean, I’m a photographer.
Of course, I’m editing and importing all the images that I put into a folder.
I didn’t test it out with importing from a device, but you can copy stuff into your library or import files to a specific place too.
Still, Capture One feels a bit more robust here as it can do a better job with multiple nested folders.
It’s at this point where I had an odd observation: why is the logo for Lightcraft a lynx?
With that aside, I went into editing.
Let me tell you, the render preview is CRAP.
I tried to mess with the settings in the menu to do this and ended up just not bothering too much.
But in Capture One, images from a Leica M11 look nice and crispy.
They sometimes even made me wonder if I got an image in focus when I know for a fact that I did.
While testing the product for an entire morning, I noted that it’s very hard to sort my images.
It works similar to how Lightroom does which is to pick or reject.
But in Capture One, I use it based on a few things.
In-camera, I give everything a star rating.
Then I further cull by using color flags.
And finally I weed the green images out and work on those.
